evidence: Judged “You were too busy avoiding pain, reading what was dangerous and what you had to do to stay in a good bond, etc.” against his line (“when childhood is organized around avoiding pain and preserving attachment, attention goes into reading danger, meeting expectations, and keeping the bond”) and the sentence it replaces (“You were too occupied in not being in pain, reading out what was dangerous and what you had to do to stay in a good bond, etc.”). The mend takes his “avoiding pain” for Emulate’s “not being in pain”, drops the stray “out” from “reading out”, and “too busy” for “too occupied in” repairs the grammar. Everything else (“You were”, “a good bond”, “etc.”) is the replaced sentence’s own wording, and the lead-in sentence in CONTEXT (“in your childhood you didn’t spend enough attention in finding out what you like...”) is what sets up the second person. Nothing is added to or taken from the meaning of the sentence it replaces. One mismatch to record, not a change of meaning: the_change says the mend uses his “reading danger”, but the draft keeps “reading what was dangerous” (Emulate’s words without “out”), which says the same thing; the description is slightly off, the draft is fine. Tell rows all ABSENT; I checked T22 and T06 (it explains a pattern in terms the article already uses, with no reassurance) and C02 (“You” is the reader of the section). Lint: D9 accepted (his line put back in a one-sentence change). E36/E41 (8.7 “you” per 100 of my words) accepted: the section speaks to the reader as “you” by design (“You are in the first camp if:”) and the replaced sentence already had the same two “you”s, so the change adds no second person.
